1	# Reader-pleasure pass
2	
3	Use this file when the user asks whether the paper is enjoyable, compelling, elegant, a pleasure to read, or when a full-section revision has already passed the logic, paragraph, and line-edit checks. The copyediting pass runs after this one, so this is not a prerequisite. This pass is about reader experience, not decoration. It must never outrank the hard constraints in `SKILL.md`.
4	
5	A research paper is a pleasure to read when the reader always knows why the next sentence is worth reading. The goal is not charm, flourish, or a magazine voice. The goal is earned momentum: each sentence reduces effort, creates a question the next sentence answers, or delivers a payoff the section has prepared.
6	
7	A research paper is delightful when the reader feels their understanding growing sentence by sentence. That is the link to the exposition pass (`references/exposition.md`): pleasure and teaching are the same property felt from two sides. A delightful paragraph usually does at least one of these:
8	
9	- resolves a question the previous paragraph opened
10	- gives a name to something the reader had only sensed
11	- turns an abstract claim into a concrete mechanism
12	- shows why a familiar assumption fails
13	- lets a result change the reader's view of the problem
14	- gives the reader a sentence they can repeat to explain the paper to someone else
15	
16	The last test matters most: if no sentence in the introduction is repeatable, the paper is hard to remember. Do not manufacture a quotable line; surface the one the paper already earns.
17	
18	## Pleasure test
19	
20	Read the revised text cold and ask five questions.
21	
22	1. **Orientation.** Can the reader state the local question by the end of the first sentence or two?
23	2. **Momentum.** Does each sentence make the reader want the next one because it opens, narrows, or resolves a concrete question?
24	3. **Payoff.** Do paragraphs end on the point the reader should remember, not on a citation, caveat, or procedural detail?
25	4. **Texture.** Does the prose mix explanation, evidence, and interpretation, or does it flatten into a list of claims?
26	5. **Relief.** After dense technical material, does the text give the reader a short synthesis sentence, example, or signpost before increasing complexity again?
27	
28	If the answer to any question is no, fix the highest-leverage sentence or flag the problem in `Diagnosis`. Do not perform a decorative rewrite.
29	
30	### The tired-reviewer read
31	
32	The five questions above are a cold read for what works. Run one adversarial variant to find what fails: read the text as a tired reviewer at 11pm and mark every sentence where your attention drops, quoting each one. A model is far better at diagnosing dead prose than at avoiding it while generating, so this diagnostic pass catches airless sentences that the drafting pass wrote past. Each marked sentence is a `Diagnosis` item, routed to the load-variation and stress-position moves below; do not rewrite from the mark alone. At paper scale this pass is the delight audit in `references/cold-read.md`; run it there for a whole-paper read and here for a single section.
33	
34	## Load variation: not every sentence should work equally hard
35	
36	Dense prose has a specific cause. When each sentence is written to convey maximum information, every sentence works equally hard, and prose that never varies its load exhausts the reader even when every sentence is true. Human writing that flows varies the load: some sentences carry the argument, others orient the reader, restate a point so it lands, or exist only to move from one idea to the next. A sentence that does nothing but transition is not filler; it is the relief that lets the next high-load sentence register.
37	
38	Concrete moves, all within the author's existing material:
39	
40	- **Let low-load sentences exist.** After a dense technical sentence, a short sentence that only names the consequence or orients the reader earns its place by setting rhythm (the keep-test's "sets rhythm" clause, `references/subtraction.md`). Do not compress it away as redundant.
41	- **Vary sentence length deliberately.** Land a point with a short sentence after a long one; build a complex idea across a long sentence after several short ones. Uniform length is itself an AI tell (`references/sentence-patterns.md`, "Sentence-length variety").
42	- **Open each section with a sentence a non-specialist could follow**, before the machinery arrives (the reader ladder, `references/exposition.md`).
43	
44	## The running example
45	
46	For delight specifically, a single example threaded through the whole paper does more than any sentence-level move. One example the reader meets in the introduction and follows through method, results, and discussion gives them a fixed handhold as the abstraction rises, and it is the most reliable source of the repeatable sentence the pleasure test asks for. Diagnose it: does the paper reuse one concrete case, or introduce a fresh disposable example in each section?
47	
48	This move is bounded by constraint 1. The editor may surface an example the author already wrote and thread it more consistently across sections the author already connects, and may point out where a scattered set of examples could become one. The editor may not invent a running example, extend one into a section where the author did not use it, or manufacture the connective claims that would carry it. When the paper would benefit from a running example it does not have, that is an `Author questions` item, not an edit.
49	
50	## Edit moves that create pleasure without hype
51	
52	- **Make the question visible.** Replace generic openings with the specific puzzle, contrast, or uncertainty the paragraph resolves.
53	- **Put the payoff in stress position.** End sentences and paragraphs on the idea that should stay with the reader.
54	- **Use concrete anchors.** After an abstract claim, give the reader a method step, dataset feature, example, failure mode, or measured outcome already present in the text.
55	- **Vary sentence weight.** Follow a long technical sentence with a short sentence that names the consequence.
56	- **Let transitions carry thought.** Use cause, contrast, sequence, or scope from the content itself rather than a stock transition word.
57	- **Preserve useful surprise.** If the section contains a counterintuitive result or tension, do not smooth it away. Frame it so the reader sees why it matters.
58	- **Prefer memorable exactness to decorative adjectives.** A precise noun or verb beats a praise word.
59	
60	## Exemplars and transferable techniques
61	
62	Use exemplars as technique sources, not as voices to imitate. The editor should borrow the move, not the mannerism.
63	
64	| Exemplar | Transferable technique | What to check in a mundane paper |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| Coase and Akerlof | Open with a puzzle or market failure the reader can feel before the literature review begins. | Does the first paragraph make the reader want an answer, or does it only announce a topic? |
67	| Schelling and Hirschman | Use a concrete case or analogy to carry abstract structure, then mark where the analogy stops. | Does an example rule out a mistaken interpretation, or is it merely decorative? |
68	| Kleinberg and Roth | Put the question before the model, theorem, algorithm, or design machinery. | Can a reader say why the machinery matters before seeing the machinery? |
69	| Lampson and Brooks | Give memorable names to ideas the reader must carry across the paper. | Are contribution lists and design principles named, or only numbered? |
70	| Chetty | Make figures and captions carry the spine of the empirical argument. | Could a skimmer understand the main empirical result from figures and captions alone? |
71	| Varian and Angrist-Pischke | Teach the intuition before the complication, then use examples to discipline interpretation. | Does the prose build the simple version before caveats and robustness details arrive? |
72	| Dijkstra and McCloskey | Let exact claims do the work instead of promotional language. | Can importance-signaling adjectives and verbs be replaced by mechanisms or results? |
73	
74	The common pattern is not literary flourish. These writers make ordinary material pleasurable by reducing reader effort at the right moments and increasing reader curiosity at the right moments. They orient before they formalize, name what must be remembered, make examples do argumentative work, let figures carry evidence, and place payoffs where the reader naturally pauses.
75	
76	An author may supply their own exemplar. "Match the sentence-length variation and paragraph pacing of this" is a usable instruction; "write engagingly" is not, because it names no target. When the author pastes a passage from a writer they admire as a pacing target, treat it as a rhythm model only: match its sentence-length variation and paragraph pacing, and nothing else. Do not borrow its diction, its mannerisms, its metaphors, or its voice, and do not import any of its content. The rule that exemplars are technique sources, not voices to imitate, holds for the author's own exemplar as much as for the catalog above; a supplied passage widens what "technique" covers to include cadence, not what may be copied.
77	
78	## Anti-patterns
79	
80	These make a paper less pleasurable even when every sentence is grammatical.
81	
82	- **Correct but airless prose.** Every sentence is accurate, but none tells the reader what is at stake.
83	- **List rhythm.** Paragraphs become a sequence of similarly weighted claims, often joined by banned transitions. Two named forms of this live in `references/sentence-patterns.md`: "Accumulation instead of argument" (coordinate claims where one should depend on another) and "Paragraph-shape variety" (every paragraph in the same claim-supports-recap mold).
84	- **Delayed purpose.** The paragraph explains machinery before naming the question the machinery answers.
85	- **Payoff leakage.** The strongest idea is followed by a citation tail, a caveat that belongs earlier, or a procedural afterthought.
86	- **Over-smoothed tension.** An interesting contrast, limitation, or surprise is edited into a bland generality.
87	- **Performative elegance.** Figurative language, alliteration, triads, or dramatic phrasing call attention to the editor rather than the paper.
88	
89	## Safe boundaries
90	
91	Pleasure edits are allowed only when they preserve the author's claims, evidence, technical terms, and emphasis. If making a paragraph pleasurable would require adding a new example, explaining a missing mechanism, changing the contribution frame, or elevating a result the author did not emphasize, ask the author instead.
92	
93	At `final polish`, pleasure edits are sentence-level only: stress position, rhythm, referents, punctuation, and exact word choice. Do not move paragraphs or add new argumentative material. At `response to reviewers`, apply this pass only inside flagged paragraphs and their immediate neighbours.
94	
95	## Rationale language
96	
97	In `Change rationale`, name the reader-experience benefit precisely. Good reasons include: visible question, improved payoff, corrected stress position, reduced processing load, restored contrast, varied rhythm, varied sentence load, a low-load sentence kept for relief, a running example threaded across sections, concrete anchor, or clearer consequence. Bad reasons include: more engaging, more elegant, better flow, stronger voice, or pleasure to read with no named mechanism.

1	# Sentence patterns
2	
3	A catalog of recurring sentence-level patterns and their fixes, plus the within-paragraph cohesion mechanics that make prose flow. Load this when the sentence-level cohesion lens in SKILL.md names a flow or pattern problem and a concrete diagnosis is useful for the change rationale.
4	
5	The theory behind the cohesion moves (Williams's old-new flow, Gopen and Swan's reader-expectation positions) lives in `references/principles.md`; this file is the operational version. Several patterns (the dropped connector, stacked verb phrases, two-way -ing forms, the vague "with", one topic per sentence, complex series, and idioms and phrasal verbs) adapt rules from ASD-STE100, Simplified Technical English; `references/principles.md` maps each rule to its academic version and lists the STE rules this skill does not adopt. The AI-tell list and banned-transition policy live in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md`, not here.
6	
7	## Cohesion within the paragraph
8	
9	The patterns below fix single sentences; these three moves fix how consecutive sentences hold together. (`references/principles.md` gives the underlying theory.)
10	
11	**The given-new chain.** Place what the reader already knows at the start of a sentence and the new information at the end; the new information of one sentence becomes the given information of the next, pulling the reader forward. The common failure is front-loading a sentence with a new technical term before the reader has an anchor.
12	
13	| Before | After |
14	|---|---|
15	| Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors were computed. The HC3 variant was used for its small-sample properties. | We computed standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity. Among the variants, HC3 performs best in small samples, so we used it. |
16	
17	Diagnostic: for each sentence, ask whether it opens on something the previous sentence established. Build transitions from this chain (end a sentence on the term the next will pick up) rather than from a transition word bolted on top.
18	
19	**Topic strings.** Within a paragraph, the subjects of consecutive sentences should form a coherent set. If the subjects jump around (the data, the model, the result, the field), the reader reorients every sentence; if they stay related (the model, its parameters, its predictions, its limits), the reader stays oriented. Diagnostic: name the subject of every sentence in the paragraph. If you cannot do it in one breath, the topic string is broken.
20	
21	**Sentence-length variety.** A run of uniform-length sentences reads mechanically, and uniform length is itself an AI tell. Vary the rhythm: land a point with a short sentence after a long one, build out a complex idea with a long sentence after several short ones. This is not mechanical alternation; it means writing for the ear and reading the result aloud.
22	
23	**Paragraph-shape variety.** The paragraph-scale version of the same tell, and the stronger one. When every paragraph runs the same mold (a topic claim, three evenly weighted supporting sentences, then a "Taken together" or "In summary" restatement of the opener), the section reads mechanically even with every banned word gone, because the shape repeats. Vary it: let some paragraphs be two sentences, let the load-bearing one build across several, and cut the closing restatement when the paragraph already landed its point (a recap that only re-states the opener is the say-it-once echo, `references/subtraction.md`). This is the structural sibling of the sentence-length tell above and of "List rhythm" in `references/reader-pleasure.md`.
24	
25	## Nominalizations
26	
27	A nominalization is a noun made from a verb or adjective. Nominalizations are not bad in themselves; they are useful when the action is the topic. They become a problem when they bury the action of a sentence behind a weak verb.
28	
29	**Pattern:** Subject + form of "to be" or "conduct" or "perform" or "make" or "have" + nominalization.
30	
31	| Before | After |
32	|---|---|
33	| We performed an analysis of the data. | We analyzed the data. |
34	| There is a need for further investigation. | We need to investigate further. |
35	| A comparison was made between A and B. | We compared A and B. |
36	| The contribution of this paper is the development of a new method. | This paper develops a new method. |
37	| Our hope is that future work will provide a resolution to this issue. | We hope future work resolves this. |
38	
39	Diagnostic: scan for words ending in *-tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ity, -ness* paired with weak verbs. If the noun names an action and the verb is doing no work, fold the action into the verb.
40	
41	Exception: when the nominalization names the topic and the action is genuinely secondary, leave it. "Our analysis of the corpus revealed three patterns" is fine; "analysis" is the topic.
42	
43	## Throat-clearing openings
44	
45	Throat-clearing is the academic habit of starting sentences with phrases that announce what is about to happen rather than saying it.
46	
47	| Throat-clearing | Direct |
48	|---|---|
49	| It is important to note that the effect is small. | The effect is small. |
50	| It should be emphasized that participants varied widely. | Participants varied widely. |
51	| One thing to keep in mind is that the data are skewed. | The data are skewed. |
52	| What we want to argue here is that X causes Y. | X causes Y. |
53	| It is worth pointing out that prior work has neglected this. | Prior work has neglected this. |
54	
55	Diagnostic: if you can delete the opening clause and the sentence still says what it means, delete it. The opening clause was telling the reader what was about to happen rather than telling them what is so.
56	
57	## Existential and expletive constructions
58	
59	"There is", "there are", "it is", "it was" used as dummy subjects. They are not wrong, but they put the topic in the wrong place.
60	
61	| Before | After |
62	|---|---|
63	| There are several reasons that motivate this work. | Several reasons motivate this work. |
64	| It is the case that the model overfits on small datasets. | The model overfits on small datasets. |
65	| There exists a tradeoff between recall and precision. | Recall and precision trade off against each other. |
66	| It is clear that further work is needed. | (Delete; if it is clear, you do not need to say so.) |
67	
68	Diagnostic: find "there is", "there are", "there exists", "it is", "it was". For each, ask whether the real topic is being introduced after the dummy subject. If so, restructure.
69	
70	Exception: "there" constructions are useful when the existence itself is the point ("There are exactly three solutions to this equation"). Use them deliberately.
71	
72	## The emphatic cleft habit
73	
74	An it-cleft ("It is X that Y") or a wh-cleft ("What Y does is X") splits a plain clause to spotlight one element. Used once for a genuine contrast it earns its place; LLMs reach for it by default, and it pushes the real subject rightward, delaying the verb the way "Misplaced stress" and "The interrupted clause" do. Unlike the expletive "it is" above, the fix is not deletion: the cleft encodes contrastive focus, so recast to a plain subject-verb only when that focus is not real.
75	
76	| Before | After |
77	|---|---|
78	| It is the interaction between prompt length and model size that drives the effect. | The interaction between prompt length and model size drives the effect. |
79	| What the ablation shows is that the gain comes from the reranker. | The ablation shows that the gain comes from the reranker. |
80	
81	Diagnostic: for each "It is/was X that/who ..." and "What ... is/does ...", ask whether the sentence is correcting a specific wrong alternative the reader would otherwise credit. If it is, keep the cleft; the focus is doing work. If it is emphasis by default, unfold it to subject-verb.
82	
83	## Noun pile-ups
84	
85	A noun pile-up is three or more nouns adjacent, where the reader has to guess which modifies which.
86	
87	| Before | After |
88	|---|---|
89	| User behavior analysis framework design | Design of a framework for analyzing user behavior |
90	| Survey response quality measurement instrument | Instrument for measuring the quality of survey responses |
91	| Algorithm performance evaluation methodology | Methodology for evaluating algorithm performance |
92	
93	Diagnostic: count adjacent nouns. Two is usually fine. Three is suspicious. Four is almost always wrong. (STE sets its limit at three, rule 2.1.) Fix by breaking the pile with prepositions ("of", "for", "in", "with"). Watch the mirror-image failure: too many such prepositional phrases in a row hold the verb off, which is the prepositional-chain variant under `The interrupted clause` below.
94	
95	## Two-way -ing forms
96	
97	An "-ing" word in front of a noun can be a verb acting on that noun or an adjective describing it, and the reader cannot always tell which. STE allows the "-ing" form only as a noun or a noun modifier for this reason (rule 3.5). In academic prose the form is common and usually clear; the failure is the case where both readings make sense in context.
98	
99	| Before | After |
100	|---|---|
101	| Testing conditions differed across sites. | The test conditions differed across sites. (Or, if the act of testing is meant: The way the conditions were tested differed across sites.) |
102	| Labeling errors reduced recall. | Errors in the labels reduced recall. (Or: Errors made during labeling reduced recall.) |
103	| Using a larger sample, the effect disappeared. | In the larger sample, the effect disappeared. |
104	
105	Diagnostic: for each "-ing" word before a noun, read it once as a verb ("testing the conditions") and once as a modifier ("conditions for testing"). If both readings fit the context, recast with a noun, a preposition, or a clause that names the agent. When the two readings make different claims and the context does not decide between them, ask the author which one is meant; do not pick. The third row is the dangling "-ing" opener: its implied subject (whoever used the sample) is not the sentence's subject ("the effect"). Repair it without naming an agent the text does not name, as the third row does; write "when we used" only when the passage already says the authors did it, and otherwise ask. A term of art that ends in "-ing" ("matching estimator", "boosting", "training set") is a name, not an ambiguity; leave it.
106	
107	## Hedge stacking
108	
109	Hedges (modal verbs and adverbs that qualify a claim) are useful for honesty. Stacked, they become evasive.
110	
111	| Before | After |
112	|---|---|
113	| This may possibly suggest that perhaps X causes Y. | This suggests X may cause Y. |
114	| It could be argued that one might consider the possibility that... | One possibility: ... |
115	| The results seem to potentially indicate a tendency toward... | The results suggest a tendency toward... |
116	
117	Rule: one hedge per claim, maximum; a claim too uncertain to make with a single hedge should not be made, and a claim solid enough to make takes one hedge or none. Exception: a hedge that marks genuine calibration or scope ("on the held-out set", "correlational", a qualifier that bounds the claim to what the evidence bears) is content, not filler; keep it, and count it as the claim's one hedge rather than stripping it (see the qualifier-is-content rule in SKILL.md and `references/subtraction.md`).
118	
119	## Stacked verb phrases
120	
121	Auxiliaries and modals stack into verb phrases the reader has to unpack before reaching the action: "would have been expected to have increased", "has been being used", "could be seen to be suggesting". STE forbids auxiliary chains outright (rule 3.4); here the target is the chain that does no work, the verb-phrase sibling of the hedge stack above.
122	
123	| Before | After |
124	|---|---|
125	| The estimates can be seen to have been affected by the outliers. | The outliers appear to have affected the estimates. |
126	| These features have been being used as proxies for income. | These features continue to be used as proxies for income. |
127	| The results could be seen to be suggesting a ceiling. | The results suggest a ceiling. |
128	
129	Diagnostic: count the auxiliaries and modals between the subject and the main verb. Two is ordinary ("has been shown"); three or more is a stack. Keep the tense and aspect (the second row keeps the ongoing use that the progressive "being used" expressed; "have been used" could describe use that has ended) and one marker that carries the claim's calibration: in the first row "appear to" keeps the uncertainty that "can be seen to" expressed, and in the third row "suggest" already carries it, so "could be seen to" goes. When you cannot tell whether a stacked modal marks real uncertainty or only verbosity, keep a marker and ask; dropping the last one turns a qualified claim into a categorical one. Some stacks hide an agent or a time: "the effect would have been expected to be larger" may mean "we predicted" or "theory predicts", and that difference is content, so when the rewrite would have to choose an agent or a time the original left open, ask the author rather than choosing. A modal that carries calibration counts toward the claim's one hedge (see "Hedge stacking" above).
130	
131	## Overclaiming
132	
133	The opposite failure: language stronger than the evidence supports. Where hedge-stacking dilutes a sound claim, overclaiming inflates a weak one. Both are miscalibration; the editor flags the change rather than rewriting the claim, because only the author knows what the evidence will bear.
134	
135	| Before | After (flag for the author) |
136	|---|---|
137	| X causes Y. | X is associated with Y. (Is the design causal, or correlational?) |
138	| Our method proves that ... | Our results are consistent with ... (Does the evidence prove, or support?) |
139	| This holds in all settings. | This holds on the three datasets we tested. (Was it tested beyond these?) |
140	| The model is robust. | The model's accuracy stays within 2 points under perturbation P. (Robust to what?) |
141	
142	Diagnostic: for each strong verb ("causes", "proves", "demonstrates", "establishes", "guarantees") and each universal ("all", "always", "any", "every"), check that the evidence in the section reaches that far. If it does not, surface the gap as an Author question rather than silently weakening the claim.
143	
144	## Misplaced stress
145	
146	The end of an English sentence carries emphasis. When the important word lands mid-sentence and trivia lands at the end, the sentence reads backwards.
147	
148	| Before | After |
149	|---|---|
150	| Performance dropped by 40% in the ablation experiment, as we found. | The ablation dropped performance by 40%. |
151	| The framework, which we describe in detail in Section 3, achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks. | The framework achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks; we describe it in Section 3. |
152	| Annotators agreed on 86% of items, after deliberation, which is high. | After deliberation, annotators agreed on 86% of items, a high rate. |
153	
154	Diagnostic: for each sentence, identify the most important word. Check whether it is in the stress position. If not, restructure.
155	
156	## The buried thesis
157	
158	The sentence that carries a passage's main point should be the easiest to read, not the hardest. The failure is the reverse: the takeaway arrives as the most clause-laden sentence in the paragraph, so the reader decodes syntax exactly where they most need the point to land clean. Fix by putting a character in the subject, the claim in an active verb, and any qualification in a following sentence rather than a nested clause.
159	
160	| Before | After |
161	|---|---|
162	| On this evidence the interface relocates the visible work of querying rather than demonstrably removing work: for our SQL-literate participants a verification burden survives the switch to natural language, and an NLIDB that hides the generated SQL would remove the very step these users relied on to trust the answer. | The interface moves the visible work of querying rather than demonstrably removing it. Our SQL-literate participants still had to verify the generated SQL, and an NLIDB that hid it would remove the very step they relied on to trust the answer. |
163	| The observation that performance degrades under distribution shift, which prior work had attributed to representation collapse, is shown by our ablations to instead follow from optimizer state. | Our ablations trace the performance drop under distribution shift to optimizer state, not the representation collapse prior work blamed. |
164	
165	Diagnostic: find the sentence stating the paragraph's main claim. If it is the longest or most deeply nested sentence in the paragraph, split it: lead with the claim in plain subject-verb-object order, and demote the qualifications to following sentences. Plainness is a change in syntax, not in strength: carry the evidential qualifiers and hedges through unchanged (here "visible" and "demonstrably", which bound the claim to what the study shows), or the plainer sentence asserts more than the original. This is the sentence-level form of "The load-bearing sentence is the plainest" in `references/altitude.md`.
166	
167	## The interrupted clause
168	
169	A clause keeps the reader in suspense until its core resolves: a subject needs its verb, a linking verb needs its complement, a verb needs its object, an object needs its complement, and so on for any element and the word that completes it. When an interrupting constituent opens up in one of those gaps, the reader has to hold an unfinished clause in working memory (the four-chunk budget in `references/principles.md`) until the sentence finally closes. The interrupter can be any kind of syntactic unit set into the gap: an appositive ("that question, calibration, open"), a parenthetical, a non-restrictive relative clause ("The interface, which relocates the visible work of querying, produced ..."), or an interposed adverbial, often stacked with a connective ("The results, however, when compared against the baseline, suggest ..."). What matters is the interrupter's position, in a gap the core has not yet closed, not its grammatical type; the type only tells you where the fix's trailing material should reattach. A sentence can trip this way while passing every other check: correct terminology, a topic sentence up front, no banned tell, a payoff at the end. The fix closes the gap so the core resolves without interruption: bring the stranded completing word up to the element it completes, or move the interrupting material to a trailing clause or its own sentence, always carrying that material through unchanged.
170	
171	| Before | After | Gap closed |
172	|---|---|---|
173	| Our data leave that question, calibration, open. | Our data leave open the question of calibration. | object and complement (`leave ... open`) |
174	| Those conditions, team literacy, schema design, and task framing, are the axes most likely to vary. | Those conditions are the axes most likely to vary: team literacy, schema design, and task framing. | subject and verb (`conditions ... are`) |
175	| One conjecture, untestable across studies that differ in task, interface, and population, is that the models have matured. | One conjecture is that the models have matured. That conjecture is untestable across studies that differ in task, interface, and population. | subject and verb (`conjecture ... is`) |
176	| The interface, which relocates rather than removes the visible work of querying, produced no reduction in task time. | The interface produced no reduction in task time. It relocates the visible work of querying rather than removing it. | subject and verb (`interface ... produced`); non-restrictive relative clause |
177	| The results, however, when compared against the baseline reported in prior work, suggest a smaller effect. | Compared against the baseline reported in prior work, however, the results suggest a smaller effect. | subject and verb (`results ... suggest`); interposed adverbial |
178	
179	Note how each rewrite keeps the interrupting words verbatim ("calibration"; "untestable across studies that differ in task, interface, and population"; "which relocates rather than removes the visible work of querying") and only changes where they sit, never what they claim. The gap can close either way: the first brings the stranded complement "open" up to the verb and leaves "calibration" where it was, while the others move the interrupting material to the end or the front. When a trailing phrase would dangle (in the third, "untestable ..." at the end would read as modifying "the models have matured" rather than "conjecture"), give it its own sentence with an explicit referent instead. The last two rows show the widening: a non-restrictive relative clause and an interposed adverbial are neither appositive nor parenthetical, but they open in the same subject-verb gap and take the same fix.
180	
181	### Machine-generated variants
182	
183	These three are the specifically LLM-generated forms of the interrupted clause. Each composes with a rule stated elsewhere, and each carries content that must move rather than die.
184	
185	**The first-mention gloss.** The model glosses a term at first mention by setting the definition into the subject-verb gap; this is the strongest LLM instance of the shape. "Retrieval-augmented generation, an architecture that retrieves passages before generating, underperformed the fine-tuned baseline." The gloss is real content, so it moves rather than dies: "Retrieval-augmented generation underperformed the fine-tuned baseline. The architecture retrieves passages before generating." This composes with the first-mention-versus-full-statement rule in `references/precision-budget.md`: the claim runs clean at first mention, and the definition lands once, in its own sentence or wherever the term is established.
186	
187	**The prepositional chain that holds off the verb.** No set-off constituent at all, but a chain of prepositional phrases stretches the subject and its verb apart. "The effect of the intervention on retention among first-year students in the treatment arm was small." The subject core ("The effect") and its verb ("was") sit eight words apart. Front the qualifying phrases: "Among first-year students in the treatment arm, the intervention had a small effect on retention." This is the mirror image of a noun pile-up (`Noun pile-ups` above): there, stacked nouns collapse the modifiers together; here, the prepositions that would break such a pile-up instead stretch the subject-verb gap. The diagnostic below catches both, because both leave the verb waiting.
188	
189	**The split correlative.** An embedded clause holds a correlative pair ("not only ... but also", "either ... or", "both ... and") open across the interruption. "The system not only reduces grading time, which was the original motivation, but also improves consistency." Close the correlative so its two halves sit together and demote the interrupter: "The system not only reduces grading time but also improves consistency. Reducing grading time was the original motivation." This ties to the "not only ... but also more than once in a section" tell in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md`: if closing the correlative leaves a second one nearby, recast rather than repeat.
190	
191	Diagnostic: for each sentence, trace the core of every clause it contains, embedded clauses included, and check that no interrupting constituent sits in a gap the core has not yet closed, whatever its grammatical type, and that no chain of modifiers holds a verb out of reach. Length is not the test: a single interrupting word counts when it holds the completing word out of reach (above, the lone "calibration" delays "open"), while a brief parenthetical the reader resolves without losing the core can stay. Carry the interrupting material through unchanged, since a scope or calibration qualifier is content (the qualifier-is-content rule in `references/subtraction.md`). "The buried thesis" above is this pattern applied to a paragraph's main-claim sentence; both share the plainness principle of "The load-bearing sentence is the plainest" in `references/altitude.md`.
192	
193	## The left-branching preamble
194	
195	A sibling of the interrupted clause, with the same working-memory cost (`references/principles.md`) but a different fix. Here the material sits before the core opens, not inside it: a stack of subordinate clauses runs ahead of the main subject and verb, so the reader carries the preamble unresolved until the core finally arrives. "Because the annotators disagreed on the hard cases, and given that the training set over-represents them, the model fails to generalize." The gap-closing fix does not apply, because no gap has opened yet; the core has not started. Instead, front the core and demote the preamble to a trailing clause or a following sentence: "The model fails to generalize: the annotators disagreed on the hard cases, and the training set over-represents them." As with the interrupted clause, the demoted material carries through unchanged; only its position moves. A short single preamble ("Because X, the model fails") is fine, the way a brief parenthetical is; the tell is the stack, two or more subordinate clauses held open before the core.
196	
197	Diagnostic: for each sentence, find where the main subject and verb begin. If two or more subordinate or participial clauses precede them, front the core and trail the rest. One leading clause is rhythm; a stack is a preamble. This shares the stress principle of "Misplaced stress" above (the core belongs where the reader can act on it) and the plainness of "The buried thesis".
198	
199	## One topic per sentence
200	
201	A sentence carries one topic: one claim, one step, or one relation between two things (STE rules 4.1 and Section 6). A sentence that carries two topics makes the reader decide where the first ends, and a second-language reader or a translation tool often decides wrong. Length is the symptom, not the defect, so use it only to find candidates: a sentence past about 25 words (counting a citation command, a math span, or a parenthetical as one word, as STE counts a parenthesis) is checked for a second topic.
202	
203	| Before | After |
204	|---|---|
205	| We recruited 412 participants through the panel provider, and the participants completed the survey in about 14 minutes on average, and we excluded those who failed both attention checks, which removed 38 respondents. | We recruited 412 participants through the panel provider. They completed the survey in about 14 minutes on average. We excluded the 38 who failed both attention checks. |
206	
207	Diagnostic: for each sentence past the mark, list the independent claims or steps it makes: parts that each have their own subject and verb and could be true or false, or done or not done, without the others. One relation between two things is one topic even though naming it takes "and" ("the trade-off between accuracy and latency"), and a qualifier belongs to the claim it governs. If the sentence makes two or more independent claims or steps, split it between them, carrying every qualifier and number through unchanged. A split that moves or rephrases a numerical clause is a change to a numerical claim, so it needs both checks: the number and its referent survive exactly, and the change is flagged for human review under the numerical-claim constraint in `SKILL.md` (in the table, "which removed 38 respondents" becoming "the 38 who failed" is such a change). A long sentence that carries one topic with a clean core stays: the mark finds candidates and never sets a cap, because uniform short sentences are their own tell ("Sentence-length variety" above). The rewrite in the table keeps a long-short rhythm without the original's three topics.

209	## The dropped connector
210	
211	Writers drop small words to save space: the conjunction "that", an article, a repeated verb. STE forbids it (rule 4.2, with a grammar rule on "that"). The common academic case is "that" after a verb of reporting or finding ("show", "find", "report", "observe", "assume", "note"). Without it, the reader parses the next noun as the object of the verb, then has to back up when a second verb arrives.
212	
213	| Before | After |
214	|---|---|
215	| We found the effect of tutoring on attendance was small. | We found that the effect of tutoring on attendance was small. |
216	| Prior work assumes the labels reflect the construct. | Prior work assumes that the labels reflect the construct. |
217	| Model trained on the full corpus outperforms baseline. | The model trained on the full corpus outperforms the baseline. |
218	
219	Diagnostic: after each reporting verb, check whether the noun phrase that follows could be its object ("found the effect"). If it could, and a verb follows that makes it the subject of a new clause instead, restore "that". Restore a dropped article in running prose, but the choice between "the" and "a" says which thing is meant, so take it from the context: the third row assumes the paper has already introduced one model and one baseline, and when the context does not settle which article is meant, ask in `Author questions` instead of choosing; captions, table headers, and figure labels may stay telegraphic when the venue's convention is telegraphic. Short objects that cannot mislead ("We found it was small") need no "that".

252	## Idioms and phrasal verbs
253	
254	A phrasal verb whose meaning is not the sum of its words ("come up with", "end up", "turn out to be", "carry out", "point out") is clear to a native reader and opaque to many second-language readers and translation tools (STE rule 9.3). Where a single verb carries the same meaning with equal precision, use it.
255	
256	| Before | After |
257	|---|---|
258	| We came up with a scoring rule. | We devised a scoring rule. |
259	| The gain turned out to be smaller in the second wave. | The gain was smaller in the second wave. |
260	| Most respondents ended up choosing the default. | Most respondents chose the default. |
261	
262	Exceptions: a phrasal verb that is a term of art or the plain verb of the field ("rule out", "set up" for an experiment, "drop out" for attrition) stays, and so does one whose single-verb replacement is longer, rarer, or less precise ("find out" is often clearer than "ascertain"). Some phrasal verbs carry meaning their single-verb replacement drops: "turned out to be" can mark a surprise, and "ended up" can mark an outcome reached after deliberation or against an expectation. The rows above assume the context shows no such meaning; when it does, or when you cannot tell, the meaning is content, so keep the phrasal verb or ask. This pattern never licenses swapping a plain word for a Latinate one: the "use, not utilize" rule in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md` still holds.
263	
264	## Vague abstractions
265	
266	Abstract nouns that hide the underlying concrete claim. Common offenders: "aspects", "factors", "issues", "considerations", "elements", "things", "approaches".
267	
268	| Before | After |
269	|---|---|
270	| Several factors influence the result. | Three things influence the result: A, B, and C. |
271	| Various aspects of the problem need consideration. | (Name the aspects.) |
272	| There are issues with the methodology. | (Name the issues.) |
273	| Different approaches have been proposed. | (Name them, or summarize their shared logic.) |
274	
275	Diagnostic: when you see one of these abstract nouns, ask what concrete content it stands for. If you cannot answer, the writer probably could not either. Flag as an author question.
276	
277	**Vague verbs** are the verb form of the same problem: "address", "handle", "deal with", "tackle", "affect", "impact", "involve", "examine", "explore", "focus on", "look at". Each stands for a more specific action, and STE's demand for a specific word (the reason its dictionary gives each verb one meaning) applies here. The specific verb usually makes a different claim: "address the confound" can mean "measure", "control for", "bound", or "eliminate", and those are four different results.
278	
279	| Before | Rewrite, unless the manuscript says elsewhere | Author question |
280	|---|---|---|
281	| We address selection bias with a reweighting step. | Unchanged. | Does the reweighting reduce, bound, or remove the bias? |
282	| Income affects turnout. | Unchanged. | Which direction, and is the design causal? |
283	
284	Diagnostic: for each vague verb on a claim, ask what the author did or found. If the passage says so elsewhere, use that verb; if it does not, the choice is substance, so ask in `Author questions` rather than picking the strongest verb.

286	## Misused connectives
287	
288	Common errors with logical connectives that obscure argument structure.
289	
290	- **"However"** signals contrast. If the next sentence does not contrast with the prior one, do not use it.
291	- **"Thus", "therefore", "hence"** signal logical consequence. If the next sentence does not follow logically, do not use them.
292	- **"Indeed"** signals confirming evidence. It is overused as a generic intensifier.
293	- **"While"** is ambiguous between "during" and "although". Prefer "although" or "whereas" for the contrastive meaning, especially in academic prose. "Since", "as", and "once" carry the same two-sense risk; the full rule is "One word, one sense" in `references/copyediting.md`.
294	
295	Note: the banned-transition list in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md` is the canonical source. The above are about misuse of allowed connectives, not bans.
296	
297	## The vague "with"
298	
299	"With" can attach a whole clause to a sentence without saying how the two relate: "Accuracy rose to 91%, with recall on rare classes falling to 40%." The reader cannot tell whether the second fact contrasts with the first, causes it, or only happened at the same time. STE limits "with" for this reason (its grammar rule on "with"). In academic prose the absolute "with X doing Y" construction is the usual case, and LLM drafts reach for it often.
300	
301	| Before | After |
302	|---|---|
303	| Accuracy rose to 91%, with recall on rare classes falling to 40%. | Accuracy rose to 91%. Recall on rare classes fell to 40%. (Flag: are these a trade-off, or independent?) |
304	| Turnout fell in rural districts, with polling places closing in 30 counties. | Turnout fell in rural districts. Polling places closed in 30 counties. (Flag: are the closures in those districts, and do they explain the fall?) |
305	
306	Diagnostic: for each "with" followed by a noun and an "-ing" or past-participle verb, name the relation (contrast, cause, place, time, manner) and use the word that states it. The license is the same as for "Accumulation instead of argument" below: make explicit only a relation the author's text supports. Two numbers moving in opposite directions do not by themselves make a contrast: in the first row "but" would present the recall drop as a trade-off against the accuracy gain, which is a claim about the result, so it needs the paper to say so. In the second row the text likewise supports no relation: "because" would add a causal claim and "where" a claim about location, since the 30 counties may lie partly outside the rural districts. When no relation is supported, keep the two facts as two sentences and ask the author in `Author questions` which relation they mean. "With" in its plain senses ("trained with dropout", "participants with a degree") is fine.
307	
308	## Accumulation instead of argument
309	
310	Banning "Furthermore", "Moreover", and "Additionally" (`references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md`) removes the word, not the habit under it: claims strung together as coordinate equals when one actually causes, enables, or qualifies the next. Delete the connective and the flat list is still there.
311	
312	| Before | After |
313	|---|---|
314	| The baseline fails on rare classes. Our method reweights them. Additionally, accuracy improves. | The baseline fails on rare classes, so our method reweights them; accuracy improves as a result. |
315	| Annotators disagreed on the hard cases. The training set over-represents them. Moreover, the model inherits the noise. | Because annotators disagreed on the hard cases that the training set over-represents, the model inherits the noise. |
316	
317	Diagnostic: for a run of same-shaped declaratives joined by additive connectives or by nothing, ask what relation actually holds between them: does one cause, enable, qualify, or contrast with the next? Name that relation with the connective that fits (because, so, but, despite). The license comes from the author's own material: a juxtaposition that already implies the relation may be made explicit, but a relation the text does not support is new substance, so flag it in `Author questions` rather than inventing it. When the items are genuinely independent, an explicit list is more honest than additive glue. The test is whether reordering the sentences changes the meaning; if it does not, they are being accumulated, not argued. See "List rhythm" in `references/reader-pleasure.md`; for why a draft defaults to this equal-weight mold, see "Why the defensive draft reads flat" in `references/precision-budget.md`.
318	
319	## Complex series
320	
321	An inline series is hard to parse when its items are long, contain their own commas, or have internal structure of their own. STE's answer is a vertical list (rule 4.3). Academic prose has two lighter answers that keep the paragraph intact: label the items, or separate them with semicolons.
322	
323	| Before | After |
324	|---|---|
325	| Participants were excluded if they failed the attention check, completed the survey in under three minutes, which we set as one third of the median time, or gave the same answer to every grid item. | Participants were excluded if they (i) failed the attention check, (ii) completed the survey in under three minutes, which we set as one third of the median time, or (iii) gave the same answer to every grid item. |
326	
327	Diagnostic: a series of three or more items where any item contains a comma or its own clause takes labels "(i), (ii), (iii)" or semicolons between items. Labels and semicolons are sentence-level edits and run at any stage. Converting a series to a vertical list changes the paragraph's shape, so it is structural: propose it in `Diagnosis` at `first draft`, never perform it at `final polish`, and only where the venue style uses lists in running text. When the items are meant to be remembered rather than parsed, name them instead (`references/edit-checks.md`, check 7).

330	
331	Pronouns and definite articles that point at things the reader cannot identify.
332	
333	| Before | After |
334	|---|---|
335	| This is a problem for downstream applications. | This ambiguity is a problem for downstream applications. |
336	| The result was unexpected. | The accuracy result was unexpected. |
337	| It suggests a different mechanism. | The 40% drop suggests a different mechanism. |

339	The "this + noun" rule: when "this" begins a sentence, almost always follow it with a noun summarizing what "this" refers to. "This finding suggests..." not "This suggests...".

341	Diagnostic: for each "this", "that", "it", "they", "the X", ask whether the reader, reading linearly, can identify the referent without backtracking. If not, supply a noun.

343	## Voice issues that matter (and ones that do not)
344	
345	The blanket prohibition on the passive voice is wrong. The passive is useful when:
346	
347	- The receiver of the action is the topic. ("The samples were stored at 4°C." The samples are the topic, not whoever stored them.)
348	- The agent is unknown or uninteresting.
349	- Old-new flow requires the receiver to come first.
350	
351	The passive is harmful when:
352	
353	- It hides agency the reader needs to see. ("It was decided that the protocol would be revised." By whom?)
354	- It produces weak verbs and nominalizations.
355	
356	Diagnostic: when you see a passive, ask whether the agent matters and whether the receiver is the topic. If the agent matters and is hidden, fix it. If the receiver is the topic, leave it.
357	
358	Similarly: "I" and "we" are not banned in modern academic prose. "We analyzed" is almost always better than "An analysis was performed".
359

1	# Subtraction
2	
3	Load this when a pass is mainly about length, when the user invokes a Strunk-and-White or "80% rule" cut, or when deciding whether to remove any unit larger than a phrase. The diagnostic lens in SKILL.md says what good prose looks like; this file says how to remove what does not serve the story without removing what does.
4	
5	Subtraction is the highest-yield edit and the easiest to botch. "Omit needless words" is a goal, not a test. The damage happens when an editor cuts by instinct or by quota instead of by a test for what each unit is doing.
6	
7	## Two operations, two risk levels
8	
9	Separate them, because "be concise" hides the difference.
10	
11	- **Compress.** Say the same thing in fewer words: a verb for a nominalisation, "because" for "due to the fact that", the deleted throat-clearing opener. Information content is preserved, so compression is near zero-risk. Apply it freely; it is most of the cut.
12	- **Delete.** Remove a unit (sentence, example, caveat, paragraph, section) entirely. This changes what the text says, so it carries real risk. Apply the keep-test first.
13	
14	Rule of thumb: compress freely, gate deletion.
15	
16	## The 80% is a prior, not a quota
17	
18	Most drafts carry 15 to 25% that does not serve the story, so expect to cut and look for the cut actively. That expectation is a healthy prior. It turns destructive the moment it becomes a number you must hit: to make quota, you start cutting load-bearing tissue out of a draft that was already tight. Cut by test and let the total land where it lands. A lean draft might yield 5%, a padded one 40%. Never manufacture cuts to reach a target.
19	
20	## The keep-test
21	
22	Before deleting any unit, ask: if this goes, what does the reader lose? A unit earns its place if it does at least one of these.
23	
24	1. **Advances the thesis.** It carries a step of the main argument.
25	2. **Makes a claim believable.** Evidence, or an example that rules out a misreading. An example that only illustrates a claim the reader already accepts is cuttable; one that rules out an alternative is load-bearing (see `references/edit-checks.md`, check 4).
26	3. **Links two ideas** the reader would not otherwise connect. The value is the link, not new information; cutting it breaks logical flow even though the sentence "said nothing new".
27	4. **Serves a reader the other sentences do not.** The plain-language gloss the non-expert needs. Removing it tightens the prose for the specialist and loses the generalist (the layered-audience rule in `references/edit-checks.md`).
28	5. **Pre-empts a predictable objection.** The caveat or limitation that stops a reviewer. It looks like weakness and reads as competence.
29	6. **Sets rhythm.** A short sentence that lets the reader breathe after a dense passage. Prose is not only information.
30	
31	If a unit does none of these, cut it. If it does exactly one, compress it but keep it.
32	
33	## The keep-test is also the catalog of destructive cuts
34	
35	Every common way a cut goes wrong is a keep-criterion the cutter did not check.
36	
37	- Cut a hedge that was calibration, not filler, and you broke criterion 2: the claim is now an overclaim.
38	- Cut a transition that "added nothing new" and you broke criterion 3: the thread is gone.
39	- Cut a "redundant" plain restatement and you broke criterion 4: the non-expert is lost.
40	- Cut the limitations paragraph because it looked like weakness and you broke criterion 5: you invited the desk reject.
41	- Cut an example that ruled out a reading and you broke criterion 2: the reader no longer believes you.
42	- Salami-slicing: ten individually safe cuts compound into the removal of a whole inferential step. The read-cold pass in SKILL.md is the check that catches the compounded loss; run it after any heavy cut.
43	
44	## Say it once
45	
46	A finding does not get clearer by being stated twice. When a later sentence restates, in fresh words, a result the reader has already read and adds nothing, one of the two goes. Keep the clearer or more load-bearing statement and cut the other. Usually that is the first, but not always: when the first statement is dense and the restatement is the plain-language gloss a non-expert needs (criterion 4) or a deliberate low-load sentence that sets rhythm (criterion 6), the restatement is the keeper and the dense original is what compresses or goes. What always goes is the true echo, the "here is what it means" sentence that only reflects the finding back and serves no reader the first did not.
47	
48	Distinguish an echo from a genuine next step, and from a distinct second claim. "Accuracy fell 18 points" followed by "so the speed gain did not translate into more correct answers" is an inference the first sentence did not state, and the keep-test keeps it (criterion 1). "Accuracy fell 18 points" and "the drop was not statistically detectable" are also two different claims, a magnitude and an inferential status, and both stay. The echo is narrower than either: "accuracy fell 18 points, a difference that was not statistically detectable" followed by "the interface produced no detectable accuracy gain" states the inferential status twice, and the restatement goes.
49	
50	## Filler qualifiers and scope qualifiers
51	
52	The qualifier-is-content rule protects scope and calibration qualifiers: "on the held-out set", "correlational", "in our sample" bound a claim to what the evidence bears, so removing one changes the claim and counts as a deletion. Other qualifiers bound nothing and only pad the sentence. The two look alike, so one test decides every case, and no phrase is filler by its wording alone: does the qualifier rule out a reading the reader would otherwise take? If it does, it is scope and it stays; if it does not, it is filler and compresses away freely. When the answer is unclear, treat it as scope and keep it, since cutting a real scope qualifier is the costlier error (criterion 2).
53	
54	The same phrase lands on either side depending on the claim it modifies, so read it out in context rather than matching the word:
55	
56	- "At this sample size" is filler beside a reported point estimate (every result is at its sample size), but scope beside a null or near-null result, where it flags that the study may be underpowered and rules out "no effect in general".
57	- "Observable" is filler when everything under discussion is already measured, but scope when the manuscript contrasts observed effort with latent, unobserved effort, where "observable effort fell" is narrower than "effort fell".
58	- "To some extent" almost always limits magnitude to a partial claim ("X accounts to some extent for Y"; "this to some extent explains the trend"): cutting it strengthens a partial claim into a full one, so treat it as scope, not filler.
59	- A dataset-scope qualifier ("in our data", "in our sample") is almost always scope: it bounds the claim to the data observed even with no contrast stated nearby, so cutting it broadens the claim past the data.
60	
61	The reading-out test is the arbiter in every row. Cut on what the qualifier does to the claim, never on the qualifier's wording.
62	
63	In an abstract, an introduction, or a contribution paragraph wherever it sits, a qualifier that is scope, not filler, has one more option beyond staying: deferral to the section that establishes the claim, with at most one forward pointer left behind. That move is governed by the refinement-vs-retraction test in `references/precision-budget.md` and counts as a relocation under the altitude gates, never a cut; the reading-out test still runs first, and an epistemic hedge on a central claim is not deferrable at all.
64	
65	## Scale the action to the unit size
66	
67	The bigger the unit, the more a wrong cut costs, so the more the editor proposes rather than performs.
68	
69	- **Word or phrase.** Cut in the rewrite.
70	- **Sentence.** Cut and log what was lost in `Change rationale`; the hard rule against silent deletion already requires this.
71	- **Paragraph or section.** Propose in `Diagnosis`, do not perform: "Section 5.2 restates the argument of Section 3; consider cutting." A structural cut is a claim about the paper's architecture, and only the author knows whether the unit is doing quiet work elsewhere.
72	
73	The revision stage still binds. At `final polish`, compress only and propose no deletion larger than a phrase. At `first draft`, you may perform sentence cuts and propose larger ones. At `response to reviewers`, cut only inside the flagged paragraphs.
74	
75	## The blind spot: subtraction never finds what is missing
76	
77	A scan that only looks for things to remove cannot find the thing that should be added: the inferential step the author skipped because the curse of knowledge made it feel obvious (Pinker, in `references/principles.md`). Sometimes the highest-value edit is one sentence more, not one fewer. Pair the subtractive scan with one question from the reader's side: where would a smart non-expert get lost? The missing step is the one unit you must never cut, and now and then must supply. When you cannot supply it from the prose, flag the gap as an Author question.
78	
79	## Worked example
80	
81	Draft (about 40 words):
82	"It is important to note that the model, which we trained on the full dataset, achieved an accuracy of 91%, a result that, due to the fact that the baseline was at 78%, we consider to be a significant improvement."
83	
84	Over-cut and destructive (4 words):
85	"The model hit 91%."
86	The baseline is gone, so the reader cannot tell whether 91% is good. Criterion 2 broken; this cuts 90% but destroys the claim.
87	
88	Right cut, compress then keep what is load-bearing (16 words):
89	"The model reached 91% accuracy, against the baseline's 78%. We trained it on the full dataset."
90	The throat-clearing and "due to the fact that" are compressed away and "significant" drops as a promotional adjective, but the baseline stays because it makes the claim believable. This cuts 60% and keeps the argument. More cutting is not the enemy; cutting the wrong unit is.

1	# AI Tells and House Style
2	
3	Patterns to flag and remove. Many of these are LLM-default phrases that signal AI-generated or AI-assisted prose. Others are house style for academic manuscripts.
4	
5	## Banned transition words
6	
7	These words and phrases mark text as AI-generated or as lazy academic filler. Remove them and rebuild the transition from the content itself.
8	
9	- Furthermore
10	- Moreover
11	- Crucially
12	- Importantly
13	- Notably
14	- Ultimately
15	- Delving (and "delve into", "delving into")
16	
17	## Banned hedging phrases
18	
19	- "It's worth noting that..."
20	- "It is important to note that..."
21	- "That said..."
22	- "Having said that..."
23	- "It should be mentioned that..."
24	
25	If a point is worth making, make it. Do not announce that you are about to make it.
26	
27	## Banned promotional adjectives
28	
29	Promotional adjectives perform certainty rather than earning it. If the substance of the sentence survives without the adjective, the adjective was throat-clearing.
30	
31	- important (the adjective; "Importantly" as a transition is also banned)
32	- novel
33	- interesting
34	- significant (except where it means statistically significant)
35	- crucial (the adjective; "Crucially" as a transition is also banned)
36	
37	Edit move: delete the adjective and reread the sentence. If the substance survives, leave it deleted. If the sentence collapses, the underlying claim was weak; flag in Author questions rather than restoring the adjective.
38	
39	## More filler adjectives
40	
41	These join the promotional list above. Each has a legitimate technical use; the ban is on the decorative use. Apply the same test: delete the word, reread, and leave it deleted if the substance survives.
42	
43	- comprehensive (legitimate only when the coverage is literally exhaustive: "a comprehensive survey of all 412 papers")
44	- holistic, multifaceted (almost always decorative; name the facets instead)
45	- nuanced (show the nuance; do not label a claim as nuanced)
46	- key, central, vital, pivotal (as in "a key insight", "a vital factor"; usually deletable, or replace with the specific reason the thing matters)
47	- rich, deep, powerful, vast (as generic intensifiers)
48	- seamless, streamlined (rarely true; describe what actually happens)
49	
50	## Importance-signaling verbs
51	
52	These verbs tell the reader that something matters instead of showing why. They are the verb form of the promotional adjectives.
53	
54	- underscores, highlights, emphasizes (when the object is "the importance of" or "the need for")
55	- showcases, demonstrates the importance of, speaks to
56	- "plays a [key / central / crucial / vital / pivotal] role in"
57	
58	Edit move: replace the signal with the mechanism. "X underscores the importance of Y" becomes "X fails whenever Y is absent", or whatever the concrete relationship is. If you cannot name the mechanism, the sentence was asserting importance it had not earned; flag it in Author questions.
59	
60	Exception: "highlights" is fine in its literal sense ("Figure 2 highlights the outlier region in red").
61	
62	## Banned framing phrases
63	
64	- "We show that...": replace with the result itself. "We show that X improves accuracy by 12 points" becomes "X improves accuracy by 12 points."
65	- "It is well known that...": if it is well known, say it; if it is not, cite it.
66	- "In this paper, we propose..." in any sentence after the contribution paragraph: repeating the frame signals the paper is still selling instead of doing.
67	
68	McCloskey on economists and Dijkstra on computer scientists both argued that rhetoric which announces its own importance signals weak content.
69	
70	## Em-dashes
71	
72	Do not use em-dashes in this manuscript. (The em-dash character itself is intentionally not printed here; replace any instance with one of the following.) The em-dash has become an LLM tell because models reach for it as a default when the right move is one of:
73	
74	- A comma, when the parenthetical is short and tight
75	- Parentheses, when the aside is genuinely separable
76	- A colon, when the second clause expands or specifies the first
77	- Two sentences, when both halves can stand alone
78	
79	Every em-dash in a draft should be replaced with one of these alternatives.
80	
81	## Inflated noun phrases and dead metaphors
82	
83	- "the landscape of X", "the X landscape", "the realm of", "the world of", "the sphere of"
84	- "a myriad of", "a plethora of", "a wide array of", "a host of", "a wealth of" (replace with a count or with "many")
85	- "rich tapestry", "tapestry of", "mosaic of"
86	- "the intersection of X and Y" (fine when two literatures genuinely meet; decorative when it just means "X and Y")
87	- "paradigm shift", "game-changer", "sea change", "watershed moment"
88	- "in today's [fast-paced / data-driven / increasingly digital] world" and other scene-setting openers
89	
90	Edit move: replace with the plain count, the specific object, or nothing. "A myriad of factors" becomes "four factors" when you can name four, and gets cut when you cannot.
91	
92	## Template sentence shapes
93	
94	LLM prose falls into a few rhetorical molds. Used once, deliberately, any of these is fine; as a reflex they flatten the writing.
95	
96	- The false-modesty antithesis: "It is not just about X, it is about Y." / "This is not merely X; it is Y."
97	- The range-gesture opener: "From X to Y, [sweeping claim]."
98	- "Not only ... but also ..." more than once in a section.
99	- "Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly" for a list meant to be remembered. Name the items instead (see `references/edit-checks.md`, check 7).
100	- The decorative triad: three parallel items where two would do or a real list is needed (see the rule-of-three note below).
101	- The concessive see-saw: every claim counterweighted the instant it is made, so the passage nets to zero ("While the method cuts annotation cost, it also adds overhead. Although the results are promising, further work is needed."). A real limitation is content and keeps its place (the qualifier-is-content rule, `references/subtraction.md`); the tell is the reflex of balancing every sentence, which commits to nothing. Fix: state the claim, and give a genuine limitation its own weight in its own place rather than bolting it onto the claim it undercuts.
102	
103	## Other LLM tells to watch for
104	
105	- Triadic constructions for their own sake ("clear, concise, and compelling"; "robust, reliable, and reproducible"). Real prose uses triads when three is the right number, not as decoration.
106	- Hedged confidence ("This may potentially suggest that..."). Pick a confidence level and own it. In an abstract, introduction, or contribution paragraph, run the zone-scoped hedge lexicon in `references/precision-budget.md` (may, might, could, suggest, potentially, arguably, generally, typically, in many cases, to some extent) and classify each hit as epistemic keeper, deferrable scope, or filler; these words are not banned, they are wrong only at the wrong altitude, so never blanket-delete them.
107	- Empty meta-commentary ("This paragraph discusses..."). Just discuss.
108	- The self-answering rhetorical question used as a transition ("Why does this matter? Because downstream systems inherit the bias." "What explains the gap? The answer lies in the sampling."). Posed and immediately answered, it is padding dressed as momentum and reads theatrical in academic register. State the claim directly.
109	- Aphoristic closers ("In the end, the data speaks for itself."). Endings should land specific points, not gesture at universal truths.
110	- "Navigate" as a metaphor for any non-trivial activity. People navigate ships and websites. They do not "navigate the literature on labor markets".
111	- "Leverage" or "utilize" (and "utilizes", "utilizing") as a verb when "use" would do.
112	- "Robust" as a generic positive descriptor. Robust to what?
113	
114	## Storytelling tells (decorative narrative)
115	
116	"Tell a story" is sound advice for structure and ruinous advice for surface. The
117	structural version, a spine built from the ABT, the knowledge gap, and the turn,
118	lives in `references/narrative-spine.md`. The surface version below is a set of
119	LLM tells. Banning them is what keeps a narrative pass from making prose more
120	LLM-like instead of less.
121	
122	- Manufactured hooks: "Imagine a world where...", "Imagine if...", "Picture
123	  this:", "Consider the following scenario:".
124	- Scene-setting stakes openers: "In an era of...", "In today's [fast-paced /
125	  data-driven] world", "As [field] continues to evolve...", "Now more than ever".
126	- The journey or quest metaphor for research: "our journey", "we embark", "we
127	  set out on a quest", "a deep dive into" (see also "navigate" above).
128	- Anthropomorphized data and results: "the data tells a story", "the numbers
129	  speak for themselves", "the results reveal their secrets".
130	- The dramatic reveal: "Enter [X]." as a standalone reveal, "But here is the
131	  catch:", "Here is the twist:".
132	
133	Edit move: replace the flourish with the paper's actual question or gap. The
134	narrative pull should come from structure, never from a bolted-on hook. If a
135	passage needs a hook to be interesting, the question it is built on is the part
136	that needs work.
137	
138	A load-bearing concrete instance is not a hook. The exposition pass
139	(`references/exposition.md`) and `references/edit-checks.md` check 4 both ask for
140	a specific case that the formalism generalizes and that carries the intuition. The
141	ban targets the dramatizing opener that does no work ("Imagine a world where...",
142	"Consider the following scenario:"), not the domain case itself. Keep the
143	substance of such an instance and drop the frame in front of it: lead with the
144	case ("A hiring pipeline screens applicants twice..."), not with an instruction to
145	imagine one.
146	
147	## Manuscript style preferences
148	
149	- Technical terms get defined on first use, including acronyms. Reuse the same term consistently; do not introduce synonyms for variety.
150	- Citations go inside the sentence, not at the end of a paragraph as a wall: "Smith (2020) showed X. Building on this, Jones (2022) extended Y." not "X has been shown, and Y has been extended (Smith, 2020; Jones, 2022)." For an existing wall, propose the redistribution in `Author questions`; do not perform it, since assigning citations to claims is the author's call.
151	
152	## Diagnostic checklist
153	
154	Before approving any revised passage, scan for:
155	
156	- [ ] Any em-dashes? Replace.
157	- [ ] Any banned transition words? Rebuild the transition.
158	- [ ] Any banned hedging phrases? Cut.
159	- [ ] Any banned promotional adjectives ("important", "novel", "interesting", "significant", "crucial")? Delete; verify the substance survives.
160	- [ ] Filler adjectives ("comprehensive", "holistic", "nuanced", "key", "seamless")? Delete; verify the substance survives.
161	- [ ] Importance-signaling verbs ("underscores", "highlights the importance of", "plays a crucial role")? Replace with the mechanism.
162	- [ ] Inflated noun phrases ("the landscape of", "a myriad of", "rich tapestry")? Replace with a count or the specific object.
163	- [ ] Template shapes ("not just X but Y", "From X to Y", "Firstly/Secondly")? Rewrite or name the items.
164	- [ ] Concessive see-saw (every claim reflexively counterweighted)? Commit to the claim; give a real limitation its own weight and place.
165	- [ ] Self-answering rhetorical question used as a transition ("Why does this matter? Because...")? State the claim directly.
166	- [ ] "We show that..." or "It is well known that..." frames? Replace with the claim itself.
167	- [ ] "Leverage" or "utilize" used where "use" would do? Replace with "use".
168	- [ ] "Navigate" as a metaphor for a non-trivial activity (navigating a literature, navigating uncertainty)? Replace with a plain verb for the actual action.
169	- [ ] Manufactured hook or scene-setting opener ("Imagine...", "In an era of...")? Replace with the paper's real question.
170	- [ ] Journey metaphor or anthropomorphized data ("our journey", "the data tells a story")? Cut.
171	- [ ] Triads that exist only for rhythm? Cut to two or expand to a real list.
172	- [ ] In an abstract, introduction, or contribution paragraph: hedge-lexicon words (may, might, could, suggest, potentially, arguably, generally, typically, in many cases, to some extent)? Classify per `references/precision-budget.md` (keep, defer with one signpost, or cut as filler); never blanket-delete.
173	- [ ] Topic sentence in the first two sentences of the paragraph? If not, restructure.
